title: A General Introduction to Psychoanalysis
author: Sigmund Freud
public_title: Is a slip of the tongue random, or does it mean something? | Sigmund Freud
hook: Is a slip of the tongue just a random error, or does it mean something?

source_passages.excerpt: It means, I think, that the product of the slip has itself a right to be considered as a valid psychic act which also has its purpose, as a manifestation having content and meaning.
Slips of the tongue do really occur with special frequency when one is tired, when one has a headache or when one is indisposed.

When the president with his opening words closes the session of the House of Representatives, instead of opening it, we are inclined to consider this error meaningful by reason of our knowledge of the circumstances under which the slip occurred.

Each of us knows from experience some examples of how one can forget projects which one has planned and promises which one has made, because an experience has intervened which has preoccupied one deeply.
It is actually a symptom of scientific thinking if one is content with these approximations of certainty and is able to carry on constructive work despite the lack of the final confirmation.
Now, am I unduly suspicious if I suspect that at the same moment in which psychoanalysis emerges before you, your resistance to psychoanalysis also raises its head?
It would be a mistake to believe that a science consists of nothing but conclusively proved theorems, and any such demand would be unjust.

sections.title: A slip that might say something
sections.narration: Is a slip of the tongue just a random error, or does it mean something? Sigmund Freud took the question seriously in A General Introduction to Psychoanalysis, the English edition of lectures he gave in Vienna. His startling suggestion about slips is that the product of the slip has itself a right to be considered as a valid psychic act which also has its purpose, as a manifestation having content and meaning. Imagine calling a teacher by the name of a parent, or saying the wrong word just when you wanted to say nothing. Many of us laugh and move on. Freud asks us to look again. Before we begin, a fair warning. This is a 1920 translation of lectures from an earlier era, and many of its claims are disputed. Modern psychologists explain most slips by the way the brain plans speech, with competing words getting in each other's way. We will read Freud as an influential thinker, ask what he got right, and see where his explanation goes further than the evidence.

sections.title: When tiredness explains it
sections.narration: Freud is not naive, and he admits what the simple explanation gets right. He says that slips of the tongue do really occur with special frequency when one is tired, when one has a headache, or when one is indisposed. That is a useful concession. A tired mind makes more mistakes, and no theory of hidden meaning should ignore it. You may have noticed this yourself. After a long day you mix up words or lose a name you know well. Freud's argument is that tiredness may explain when slips are likely, but not which slip appears. Why this word and not another? That is the question he wants to ask. Whether he answers it correctly is another matter, and psychologists still argue about it. The method he shows is worth borrowing, though. Start by listing the ordinary causes, such as fatigue, distraction, and haste. Only then ask whether anything is left unexplained. A good explanation begins by taking the simple causes seriously and then asking what they do not cover.

sections.title: The president and the opening words
sections.narration: Freud offers an example that has stayed with readers for a century. In his words, when the president closes the session instead of opening it, we are inclined to consider this error meaningful. He adds that this comes from our knowledge of the circumstances under which the slip occurred. The idea is that if the president privately hoped the session would end quickly, the slip says so. It is a neat story, and it shows how the theory works. The meaning is found in the circumstances. Yet this is also the weakness. We know the circumstances only after the slip, so any story can fit. A careful reader should ask whether the explanation could have been proven wrong. Modern researchers have tested slips in the lab, and found that people make errors that match the words they have just prepared or primed, with or without any hidden wish. Freud's example is memorable, but a memorable story is not the same as evidence. Enjoy it, and hold it loosely.

sections.title: Forgetting what we would rather avoid
sections.narration: Freud moves from words to memory. He writes that each of us knows from experience some examples of how one can forget projects which one has planned and promises which one has made, because an experience has intervened which has preoccupied one deeply. In plain terms, we forget what competes with something more pressing. There is a plain truth here. A worry about a family matter can push a dentist appointment out of your mind. Freud wants to go a step further and suggest that we sometimes forget what we are reluctant to do. That is more debated. Research does show that people tend to forget tasks they find unpleasant or that matter little to them, though many other things affect memory. It gives you a practical test. The next time you forget something, ask two questions. Was I overloaded, or was I avoiding it? If you were avoiding it, the useful response is to face the reluctance, perhaps by shrinking the task or giving it a fixed time. Forgetting can be a signal, and not only a failure.

sections.title: Science without final proof
sections.narration: Freud knew his ideas would be hard to prove, and he addresses this directly. He says that it is actually a symptom of scientific thinking if one is content with these approximations of certainty and is able to carry on constructive work despite the lack of the final confirmation. That sounds reasonable, and in many fields it is. Scientists often work with partial evidence while they wait for better tests. But the idea has a risk when it is used to protect a theory from criticism. A fair standard is that a theory should say what would count against it. Many critics, including the philosopher Karl Popper, argued that psychoanalysis often fails this test. Others disagree and point to parts of it that have been supported. For your own thinking, this lecture offers a balanced lesson. It is fine to hold an idea provisionally. It is not fine to hold it so that nothing could ever change your mind. Ask of any belief you cherish what observation would make you give it up.

sections.title: The trap of dismissing every objection
sections.narration: Here is a line that deserves a careful reading. Freud asks the audience whether he is unduly suspicious if he suspects that at the same moment in which psychoanalysis emerges before you, your resistance to psychoanalysis also raises its head. He is saying that disagreement may itself be a sign of discomfort. There is something to this. People do resist ideas that threaten how they see themselves. But the move has a problem, because it can be used to explain away every objection. If agreement proves the theory and disagreement shows resistance, nothing could ever count against it. This pattern is worth knowing, since it appears in many arguments, not only in psychology. When someone says your objection proves their point, be careful. A good test is whether the other side's criticism can be answered with evidence, and not only with an account of your motives. You can apply the same test to yourself. When you dismiss a criticism, ask whether you have answered it, or only explained why the critic might be biased.

sections.title: What to keep from Freud
sections.narration: We have followed Freud through six ideas: the meaning of a slip, tiredness, the president's error, motivated forgetting, science without final proof, and the problem of resistance. Keep an open mind and a habit of testing ideas. One sentence from his lectures belongs with them. He says it would be a mistake to believe that a science consists of nothing but conclusively proved theorems, and that any such demand would be unjust. That is fair as far as it goes. Science does advance through ideas that are not yet settled. It is also fair to say that an idea must eventually face tests. Remember what this book is. It is an early twentieth-century introduction, written to persuade, and later research has changed much of the picture. Read the original lectures yourself and notice where he offers evidence and where he offers interpretation. The useful ending is a precise question. What recent slip or lapse of yours has a plain explanation, and is there any part of it left that is worth a closer look? Write down one answer, and subscribe to MindLore for psychology read from the original texts.
